facts.text: In 1945 Fleming warned that taking too small a dose of penicillin could breed resistant microbes, which could then spread to other people.
By the early 1950s, about half of the Staphylococcus aureus samples taken in hospitals were resistant to penicillin.
Antibiotic resistance is a natural process: the drugs kill the bacteria that can be killed, while resistant survivors remain and multiply.
Resistance traits can be passed down from one generation of bacteria to the next and can also move directly from one germ to another.
Plasmids are circles of DNA that can move between cells and can carry resistance genes from germ to germ.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses, so they do not help with colds, flu or most sore throats.
Antibiotics also kill helpful bacteria that protect the body from infection.
In the United States, at least 30 percent of antibiotic use is unnecessary.
Antimicrobial resistance directly killed at least 1.27 million people worldwide in 2019 and was associated with nearly 5 million deaths.
In 2023, about one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections around the world was resistant to antibiotics.
Resistance belongs to the germs: it is bacteria and fungi, not the patient's body, that develop the ability to defeat the drugs.
